quote: But what set humanity firmly on the path of Science was noticing that certain modes of thinking uncovered beliefs that let us manipulate the world.
content: The essay's claim is about what "set humanity firmly on the path of Science," not about who invented the steam engine. Mokyr's own thesis in The Gifts of Athena (2002, book, no DOI) is that growth became self-sustaining after 1750 because propositional knowledge and technique began to feed each other. Engineers' failures posed questions to science, and science's answers widened what engineers could do. That feedback loop, in which acting on the world supplies an outside test of which ways of thinking work, is the essay's story. Greek natural philosophy is the essay's counterexample, not Fable's: it ran for centuries without that test and produced elegant theories of the elements that nobody could check and that went nowhere for two thousand years.

quote: it has a special and admirable purity
content: Two paragraphs later the essay makes Fable's point itself. Pure curiosity "may not linger too long on verifying its answers, once the attractive mystery is gone," which is why the essay praises instrumental goals for supplying "an outside criterion of verification." "Purity" describes the motive, which values an answer for its own sake. It says nothing about how reliable the method is. The information-gap findings describe which questions curiosity picks, not whether it tracks the truth once it has picked one, and the essay concedes the picking point too when it says a curious agent ranks questions by how they tickle its aesthetic sense. Fable has taken the essay's own qualification and presented it as an objection.

quote: (Thankfully not many have questioned what truth is.)
content: The sequence does say what it assumes, and its answer is one of the positions the note lists as a rival. The opening essay explains what "true" is for by the generalizations it allows: "There is no need to say 'it is true that snow is white' when you could just say 'snow is white.' What makes the idea of truth useful is that it allows us to talk about the general features of map-territory correspondence." That is the deflationist's account of the truth predicate. The sequence joins it to a causal story, told in The Simple Truth and The Lens That Sees Its Own Flaws, of how maps come to vary with their territories. Horwich's schema plus a causal account of reliability is the minimal commitment an epistemology needs, and the sequence takes it without pretending to more.
